summary: An official public record of an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society concerning the ONC RPC and XDR protocols. It is a legal and administrative document rather than a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A company that invented some rules and the group that looks after the Internet wrote down a deal about who looks after those rules. This memo is the signed record.

subtitle: The legal agreement that let Sun's ONC RPC and XDR specifications enter the IETF standards process.

tldr.problem: Sun Microsystems owned the ONC RPC and XDR specifications, and the IETF could not turn them into Internet standards without permission to use and change them.
tldr.mechanism: Sun grants the Internet Society and the IETF a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license for the sole purpose of making the technology an Internet standard, and promises similar no-charge licenses to implementors if it reaches Proposed Standard.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is explicitly not a standard. It is the public record of the agreement, and the section that lets the IETF evolve the technology lapses if no Proposed Standard appears within 24 months.

today: RFC 1790 is an Informational record of a 1995 agreement, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is a legal record, not a technical specification.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 1790 states that it is not a standard. It is an official public record of an agreement between Sun Microsystems and the Internet Society. The two specifications involved, RFC 1057 (RPC version 2, June 1988) and RFC 1014 (XDR, June 1987), are not attached but are incorporated by reference.

Its purpose is to permit the flow of Sun's Open Network Computing (ONC) Remote Procedure Call and External Data Representation specifications into the Internet Standards process run by the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a signed note saying a company agreed to share its rules with the Internet's rule makers. It is a record of a deal, not a rulebook.

sections.title: The License Sun Grants
sections.content:
In paragraph 1, Sun (the "Donor") grants the Internet Society and the IETF, with their officers, employees, the IETF Secretariat and contractors (the "Licensees"), a cost-free, perpetual, non-exclusive, worldwide license under any copyrights, patents or other rights. It covers using, copying, modifying, distributing and creating derivative works, and using the marks "ONC RPC" and "ONC XDR". It is granted for the sole purpose of making the technology an Internet standard, entering the process as a Proposed Standard.

Paragraph 2 gives the Licensees the right to evolve and modify the technology through the Internet Standardization Process (see RFC 1602). If Sun develops the technology outside that process, this must be clearly labeled as a non-standard development, with no reference to the Internet Standards Process.
sections.plainLanguage: Sun says the Internet group may use, copy and improve its rules for free, as long as the goal is to make them an official Internet standard.

sections.title: Licenses for Implementors and the 24-Month Limit
sections.content:
The Licensees have no duty to publish the technology or to take it onto the standards track, and they take on no confidentiality obligation. Sun states that, to the best of its knowledge, there are no infringement claims against the technology and that it was not prepared jointly with others.

If the technology becomes a Proposed Standard, Sun agrees to license it to others on substantially similar terms at no charge, so long as those licensees implement the Internet standard. If it is not elevated to Proposed Standard within 24 months of the agreement, Section 2 of the agreement is null and void. The introduction notes that people other than the named Licensees must be separately licensed, and that Sun could offer a blanket license to implementors if the RFCs are reissued as Proposed Standards.
sections.plainLanguage: If the rules become official, Sun promises to let everyone use them for free. If nothing happens within two years, the IETF loses its right to change them.

sections.title: Disclaimers, Signatures and Security
sections.content:
Sun provides the technology "as is" and disclaims all warranties, and it is not liable for lost revenue, profit, data or damages of any kind. The agreement is the entire agreement between the parties, changes must be in writing and signed, export control laws must be followed, and California law governs where no U.S. federal law does.

It was signed for Sun by Jim Bill Maier on 4-6-95 and for the Internet Society by Vinton G. Cerf on 4-11-95. The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Like most contracts, it says Sun is not responsible if something goes wrong, and it was signed by one person from each side.
